utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Marro?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Hearing on provisional release on the case IT‑96‑21‑T, the Prosecutor of this Tribunal against Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I have appearances for the Prosecutor, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning. Teresa McHenry appearing for the Office of the Prosecutor; with me is Ms. Elles Van Dusschoten who will be assisting me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: For the Defence, please, appearances?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Edina Residovic, lawyer from Sarajevo. I am the Defence counsel of Mr. Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GALIJATOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ekrem Galijatovic. I am a lawyer from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You will be appearing for the Defence as well, sir, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GALIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good, thank you. This is a hearing on the motion for provisional release filed by the Defence pursuant to Rule 65(B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal. Rule 65(B) provides that release may be ordered by a Trial Chamber only in exceptional circumstances after hearing the host country and only if it is satisfied that the accused will appear for trial and, if released, will not pose a danger to any victim, witness or other person. The Trial Chamber has received a document dated July 18th 1996 from the government of the Netherlands which sets forth its views regarding this motion for provisional release. Has the Prosecutor received a response of this statement from the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Netherlands, and has the Defence received it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I received a copy this morning, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Has the Defence received it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I received it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. Who will present the motion for provisional release? Ms. Residovic, will you present that for the accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Lordships, your Honour, before I explain in more detail our motion for the provisional release, I should also like to take the liberty and mention several facts which I believe are of relevance for this motion.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On 14th May, the Defence submitted several motions to the Court and then on May 28th, with some additions on June 5th and the 9th, it has submitted further motions relative to Rule 73 of the Court. So far, very few of these motions have been deliberated about, although their deliberation is directly related to today's motion. On May 14th the Defence submitted a motion requesting that the Court rule about the forwarding of the documents in the language of the accused. However, the Court has not yet ruled on this motion, nor have we received any answer. Whether my client may use his mother tongue in speech and writing depends also on whether he has already received the documents which are the subject of today's hearing received in that language. I must say that our client has not yet received in Bosnian language neither the ruling of this Court, nor the decision of the Dutch government in that tongue. We, therefore, are already faced with a situation which is a discrepancy with Rule 21 of the Tribunal. On June 5th and 9th, the Defence requested that evidence be exempted when it was found or taken away from the accused and the disclosure of the evidence, because on the 29th we suggested the reciprocal production of evidence under 65(B). The Prosecutor was, therefore, bound to present to us all evidence that is at its disposal which we believe are of interest to the Defence, that is, that have been received or taken away from our client. Regrettably, I must say that even though the Court with regard to one of these motions, and that the statement by the accused Zdravko Music be delivered to the client within 14 days, I only received this motion on July 2nd, that is, after 14 days and in English, even though I already stated that I speak the other official language of the Court, and the request that we be submitted these documents in Bosnian language so that my client could also get acquainted with it. We have not received it to this day. This, I believe, is also relevant to this case because 66(B) is thus converted into 66(A), and that the Prosecution decides when the Defence will be acquainted with some evidence rather than under Rule 66(B), which means that we have to be informed about that particular evidence immediately. Evidently, it appears that the Prosecution believes that something has to be hidden from the Defence and this is an infringement of my client's right. The Prosecutor has informed me in writing that as of yesterday other evidence will be presented to me now, but I must say that already two months have elapsed since I have been entitled to this evidence. We also have moved that the Prosecutor exclude some of the evidence and the provisional release could not use the evidence submitted by the client, and that is an ID card of Stjepan Kozul which was among the documentation found with him and taken away from him. We are not saying this because we might deny the existence of this identity card or that we deny that my client used that, but because for more than two months the Defence has been faced with a situation in which it cannot avail itself of the right it is entitled to. In addition to our other motions, we have submitted a large number of material evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you one moment, if I may, Miss Residovic, just so that we can have some order to the hearing. What you are telling me is there are other motions that are outstanding that have either not been resolved or the Prosecutor has not complied with. You were just beginning to tell the Chamber that with respect to the identity card that it was your position that should not be made a part of the evidence or the material that the Chamber should use in considering your motion for provisional release. So it appears that you are now beginning to address the motion for provisional release which is the purpose of the hearing. I do not want to cut you off. We have a status conference set for ‑‑ when? I am mistaken. The status conference is for two of the other accused in this case. We have had a status conference in your case. I can respond to your concerns, perhaps, or I can attempt to respond to some of your concerns, but we have allotted an hour this morning to hear argument on the motion for provisional release. So, unless it is your position that these matters somehow impact or relate to your motion for provisional release, I would prefer that we set a date ‑‑ we can do it as soon as possible even though we are in trial in another matter ‑‑ to consider all of these matters, for example, the request that you have documents in the language of the accused. It is my understanding that the Registry has responded to you. I see Mr. Marro shaking his head. We certainly discussed it and we thought that it had been resolved. As far as the statement of Mucic, you said you received that on July 2nd and then it was in English and not in the language of the accused. That is something we can follow up on. You did make a request for discovery under 66(B), as I recall from our earlier status conference. There is no way really in the present setting for the Chamber to resolve your concerns about the Prosecutor not fully complying with that. That is something that really should be resolved in a more informal setting where we can discuss back and forth. So, since we have alloted a certain amount of time for this motion for provisional release, I would appreciate it if you would address that and if there are other matters that are pending, or if you feel the Prosecutor is not fully complying with its obligation, then you should advise the Trial Chamber. It would be preferable if you would write a note to the Trial Chamber, a letter to the Registry, and the Registry would then deliver it to us, listing your concerns. We would then have an informal conference, a status conference, and try to resolve that as quickly as possible. I understand you might feel you are here and you want to have all those things resolved but, for efficiency sake, I would ask that you move to the motion for provisional release.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I can only be concerned, your Lordships, by what can affect the rights and interests of my client. That is why I drew attention to some of the previous questions for which I had asked to discuss, and I shall proceed immediately to the motion for provisional release. If the Court believes that today it cannot decide without previous deliberation about other matters which I have only indicated, then I should like to ask your Lordships to notify us of the date when we shall be able to clarify those matters. I also beg you to inform both us and the Prosecution about that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have the status conference for two of the other accused tomorrow evening. Could we meet Ms. Residovic this evening at between either 5.30 or 6.00? We normally conclude the trial for the day at 5.30. Could you remain today and then meet and see if we can resolve all of these outstanding matters regarding material that the Prosecutor was to provide and whether it is in the language of the accused or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, as far as the Defence is concerned, we can come and discuss those matters, but in view of the Defence's view that the decision on this motion depends on some of those questions, then I should like to ask you to hold another conference and that is on the motion for provisional release.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We cannot go forward and hear your argument on provisional release and then just reserve ruling until we resolve these other matters, is that a possibility, or are you saying you are not ready to present argument on your motion for provisional release until these other matters are resolved?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can present our arguments, but they presume some comments on the previous motions, since part of the material, evidence and other documentation relative to my client were submitted along with those motions, so that I can present some of the arguments if you like right now, or perhaps we could envisage it for later today or tomorrow or whenever your Lordships find it convenient?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think we would like to hear from you and you can indicate which portions of your argument you cannot fully present without a resolution of the other matters. In your motion you do make reference to an earlier motion for a separate trial, but I do not see the Prosecutor is involved in that, in that there is no material that I understand they are to provide you that relates to that motion. You have just mentioned the ID, identification document, of the accused, and that may somehow relate ‑‑ I would like, if we can hear from you, how long do you think it would take for you to present oral argument on your motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Some 10 minutes, perhaps a little longer. I cannot be more exact.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, very good. Ms McHenry, are you available this evening at 5.30 to discuss any discovery matters that Ms. Residovic was referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Then we will have a status conference this evening to resolve any of those matters. Ms. Residovic, would you proceed with your oral argument on your motion for provisional release, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In our motion in writing, we indicated that my client without any factual grounds was detained before the indictment had been filed against him. We pointed out that since the Statute of the International Tribunal knows no contingency measures, emergency contingency measures, under which my client could be detained, we believe that the provisions on contingency measures should be applied very, very strictly which I do not think was done in this case. However, since the ruling was taken subsequently, I should not go back to this particular ruling of 18th March this year. Now I should like to comment on the Prosecutor's response to the submitted motions. The Prosecutor in his response to our view that our client will respond to any summons by the Court submitted as evidence a counterfeit identity card, as the Prosecution claims, and a personal invitation for official travel. It is not a forged identity card or document, even though there is my client's picture and the name of Stjepan Kozul. I believe that your Lordships must remember that this relates to events of '92 and, unfortunately for us who live there, it was a great misfortune that these things happened, but people and especially the Muslim people and those who exercised some functions in that Muslim people, including my client, could not pass through the areas controlled by Bosnian Serbs and at that time also through to the territory controlled by Bosnian Croats with our normal documents, with Bosnian names. So we know the man who issued a request to the relevant body to issue such an identity card. We have the testimony of that witness, and the authority in the Republic Bosnia‑Herzegovina confirming that it has issued orders to all relevant authorities to issue such a document. On two occasions representatives of the HVO, that is Croatian Defence Council, attempted against the life of my client and he could not move freely in any territory whatsoever. The relevant Ministry of the Interior holds that this identity card is an agreement with the decision, with the agreement which existed between the HVO and the BH army, that is BH Ministry of the Interior. It is also said that when against my client another trial was mounted, it said there are implications that he escaped by a Chetnik helicopter. There is complete documentation in the press showing that my client stated publicly and clearly that he left Bosnia‑Herzegovina with this identity card and these documents, because the life of those people was otherwise threatened in any other way. So this is not a man who forges documents or uses forged documents. It was a legally issued document so that under wartime conditions in Bosnia‑Herzegovina the movement of people could be ensured. We can also submit all relevant evidence we have to this distinguished Chamber in English and statements of witnesses in Bosnian and they, I believe, are of the utmost relevant for our motion. The answer of the Prosecution says that my Defendant can go to some countries which are not co‑operating with this Tribunal. It mentions Serbia where his children live and Croatia where he has a large number of friends and acquaintances. We can also produce evidence clearly showing that if this Tribunal accuses my client of such severe crimes, grave crimes against Serbs, then it is absolutely out of the question ‑‑ I am sorry for using this term ‑‑ to say that my client can go to a country if he is allegedly responsible for such grave breaches. Secondly, those untruths that my client escaped to Serbia with a Chetnik helicopter, and claiming that my client was a superior issuing orders. These stories originate in the country to which the Prosecution claims that he can go now. So, this is evidently again quite impossible. The third reason why my client should not be provisionally released is that he has considerable financial means. It is quite true that over 20 years of work in various western countries, my client has indeed earned considerable assets, but he has spent all his assets as a patriot helping the struggle against fascism in those territories. Today he has to earn his livelihood and lives and has only his salary, and at present he does not have the salary. We can also submit evidence to this effect, that companies simply cannot ‑‑ the company that he works for cannot cover the expenses. His children have no means of support and cannot move from Serbia to another country which would be safer for them. So that these reasons also would prevent my client from boarding a helicopter and moving to a country which does not co‑operate. Thirdly, that we have not presented any extraordinary circumstances. We have done so from the beginning. If we look at the documents that I have already mentioned, material and other evidence, 30 statements of witnesses, numerous documents in writing, video material from the time when the events were taking place. If this Chamber hears all this, then it will realise that on the basis of such scarce evidence that is presented, it should not rule that my client should remain in detention. After all, there are two documents of relevant bodies that no proceedings have been conducted against him and that my client does not have a criminal record. If the Court imposes some additional measures, that is, a compulsory stay in a particular country or whatever, then we would take measures, make an effort to ensure that and to guarantee that my client would always respond to any summons by this Tribunal to appear before this Chamber. So these would be some of the arguments in response to the Prosecutor's response to our motion. Briefly, we have referred to the provisions relative to the detention. I should also like to add that if this Tribunal does not comply with the national legislation, however, the Criminal Proceedings Acts of Slovenia, Croatia, Yugoslavia, Macedonia stipulate the shortest term of detention and the urgent response of all the authorities, that is, the abolition of detention at the moment when grounds for the detention cease to exist.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Have you considered, perhaps, posting a bond or some other provision that might help to ensure the appearance of the accused, should he be released? There is no specific provision for that in our Rules under Rule 65, of course, but I do not know whether that is a provision that is used in your country or not. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the financial situation I have already referred to, I can already say that my client can guarantee verbally that he will appear before the Court. He can do it, and we are in contact with the authorities of Bosnia‑Herzegovina. If my client is in their territory or in the country where he presently has his residence, that is, with the authorities of the Republic of Austria, we could perhaps agree on some provisional solution that would guarantee that my client would appear before the Court whenever he is summoned. Of course, we would then need a particular period of time, a particular deadline, to know before the Court rules finally on this.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In your country, if a person who is charged with a serious crime is released on bond, assuming that there is a provision for release, is there typically a provision for that person to post a bond, an amount that would be forfeited if the person did not appear? You are shaking your head. One is shaking his head "no", one "yes". Someone tell me, please, from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GALIJATOVIC
utterances.text: In our country there is the institute of the so‑called bail and in this case, of course, the assets, the amount, is forfeited in favour of the state, if whoever fails to comply with it. But at present in our state, in Bosnia‑Herzegovina, this so‑called socialist or, rather, communist Criminal Proceedings Act is in force. It is one of the latest, one of the most advanced, criminal regulations in Europe and probably in the world too. Our criminal proceedings envisage that the Court must ex‑officio at any given moment check, verify the justification or the grounds for their detention. I do not have the documentation with me, but we are quite ready to find the means so as to pay the bail bond, the guarantee, or to lay down a deposit which the Chamber determines. As a rule, this is possible with us. Your comment, whether in such cases this is applied in our country, I can say very frankly and very openly that it is not the common practice with us. But we are typical of the Austro‑Hungarian school of thought. In 1892, it adopted the criminal proceedings law by Austria Hungary. The terms of detention were 28 hours, 48 hours, 72 hours, seven days and only in exceptional cases the detention could be longer than that. In this provision adopted in the last century, there was also another provision, and that is that every week the Presiding Judge and the President of the Bar Association had to verify the detention, pay a visit to the detainees and things like that. I must add another thing. I am rather disagreeably surprised by the indictment, by the manner in which my client was indicted. I already said that in the court of Bosnia‑Herzegovina and I can say it very responsibly. In May '92, I was one of those who proposed to establish this International Tribunal. I believed that national legislations, national political relations and all the circumstances could not bring about the punishment of real criminals for acts, for offences, which are unheard of in the history of the human kind. I also wish to say that this indictment, we have nothing against, neither I, as a lawyer, a Muslim from Bosnia‑Herzegovina, we have nothing against our people being brought to trial or being convicted of war crimes. In the course of the war, my colleague and I, we defended hundreds of criminal cases before our military courts which tried people for all violations of human rights perpetrated by the army of Bosnia‑Herzegovina. Rigorous punishments were brought against those perpetrators even for the least violations of human rights. So we have nothing against indicting and incriminating our people, but we are against the manner in which this is done. My client here is accused that since April '92 he was the Commander, he was a co‑ordinator and then, as of July, Commander of the first tactical group. So these are two completely different functions in the military and political life. But when holding either of these positions and removing from one to another, he is still responsible, even during this intermediate period when he is out of any of these positions, he is again accused or either committing or omitting to commit various things. So this shows that my client is being framed up by one of the parties to the conflict which wants Zejnil Delalic to represent as a guilty party, regardless of the position he held. Moreover, the indictment must contain evidence on his commanding position. Secondly, his knowledge about possible omissions of either the prison warden or any of his subordinates' actions and reactions. All these facts must be included in the counts of the indictment so as to be able to assess it. As it is, you do not know who he is, what he was, nor do you have any informative documents that would be showing this. You take up two statements of members of the HVO who were in conflict with Delalic and who wanted to liquidate him in order to create peril for some other detentions. Specifically, Zejnil requested himself that he would be transferred from Germany to the Tribunal in The Hague. He will appear before this court at any given moment. But I think that all elements need to be taken into consideration, especially his family situation and everything else, and to rule that he be released from the detention, but he was the one who requested to be transferred. He also asked for his urgent transfer. I do not have here, I do not want to discuss the indictment because I come from a different legal school of thought, but I think that this kind of indictment does not have the feet to stand on without any additional evidence or the analysis of the rights and duties of Zejnil Delalic and what did he do or omitted to do to prevent possible crimes that may have taken place. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I want to hear from the Prosecutor. We have received their written response as well, but the question that I have to both the Defence and to the Prosecutor is to what extent should the Trial Chamber involve itself in the merits, particularly as it relates to the position of the Defence and its motion for provisional release, that Mr. Delalic was not occupying a position of superior authority and that he is not responsible for the offences charged, alleged to have occurred, in Celebici camp. It seems to me that needs to be resolved; to what extent should this Trial Chamber, in ruling on the motion for provisional release, involve itself in the merits of the crimes charged? You have filed a motion for separate trial, Miss Residovic. I am not sure whether you filed a motion to dismiss the indictment ‑‑ have you?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not hear you. I did not quite understand what you asked me.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have filed a motion for separate trial. In your motion for a separate trial you have asked that Mr. Delalic, that his trial be severed from the trials of the other accused because he occupies a particular position that is different. The indictment charges that he co‑ordinated the activities of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat forces in the Konjic area from approximately April 1992 to at least September 1992, and was the Commander of the first tactical group of the Bosnian Muslim forces from approximately June 1992 to November 1992. His responsibilities included authority over the Celebici camp and its personnel. That, it seems to me, is the important allegation that is made. His responsibilities included authority over the Celebici camp and its personnel. When you look at the indictment, numerous ‑‑ I cannot recall how many counts ‑‑ counts are alleged, numerous crimes are charged in several counts charging individuals with committing these offences, never Mr. Delalic, but other individuals, as I recall, who were either the Commander or the Deputy Commander of the camp or guards at the camp. The Prosecutor has charged that he is responsible because he was the Commander of the first tactical group which included authority over the Celebici camp. My question is ‑‑ that is the allegation, in your motion for provisional release you are saying that he did not have this superior authority, that he did not have authority over the camp, I gather, and he is not responsible ‑‑ is this the proper time to consider that? At least in my experience, I would not consider the merits of the charges that are lodged in the indictment in deciding the motion for provisional release. Instead, a motion to dismiss the indictment would be filed saying that either he was or he was not the Commander but, even if he was the Commander, he had no responsibility. A hearing would then be had on those matters, but that is separate and apart from a motion for provisional release. Judge Stephen says that you have filed a motion based on the defects and the form of the indictment. Perhaps that is the motion that brings this issue to us. But do you understand what I am saying to both counsel? Is this the time for us to consider the merits of the indictment or instead should we look to the indictment as charging very serious offences, Mr. Delalic being from a foreign country and other circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I fully agree with you. It is not today we should discuss this matter. But I have already said our previous motions which indicate the stand of the Defence that he is not responsible for Celebici camp, neither he is the Commander of the camp or the Commander of the first tactical, they are before this Chamber. Some of them have been translated into English. The second also means whether his right to use his mother tongue includes his right to submit written documents in Bosnian. We have accepted your ruling and we agree to discuss it this afternoon. So, it is not now that we shall discuss it. But I think that your Honours have to rule whether this indictment has to be rejected on all counts or not. One hour or perhaps more will be needed to resolve that, but your direct question was answered by my colleague. We know the institute of bail bond and, as for the detention, our legislation, the legislation of all countries in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, envisages compulsory detention in case of those offences which entail death penalty. This Tribunal does not have capital punishment. In all other cases, whenever we are talking about terms of imprisonment, there is no compulsory detention. Even this provision on compulsory detention, in cases of capital punishment there is an exception. This we have in Article 191, para. 1.2 of the criminal proceedings, and detention is always ruled against persons for whom there are grounds to doubt that he has committed an offence for which the law prescribes capital punishment. If evidence shows that this case could enter milder punishment under law, then the detention need not be imposed. This is under our legislation, and so I believe I have answered your question directly now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ms McHenry, will you present argument for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Could I ask you a question? I came here thinking that you would be telling me something of exceptional circumstances and also something about why the Court should be satisfied that the accused will appear for trial. I have heard nothing on either of those critical matters which are the only matters that are relevant to this present application. I wonder whether you want to add something on those two aspects because, without them, it seems to me that your application cannot succeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try to give you the reasons and the main reason, the principal reason, is that the Prosecution has not offered any arguments that directly apply to my client, and other reasons are that the children of my client are in Belgrade. We have submitted documents, press clippings, that can show the climate there. Also, we have also said that the livelihood of about 20 members of his family is dependent on his work. If he is released now, there is no danger of him not appearing for a trial, but also we are allowing him to take care of his family which is now in Austria and other places and we will allow him to prevent further erosion of his circumstances of their living. If we go back to the other questions, maybe adverse results that may refer to this trial. I think that all these reasons are very exceptional, because the detention is an exceptional circumstance and that is the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: How old are the children?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: One is a college student, 18 years, and one is 22, I believe. I am not sure. 16 and 22.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ms McHenry, would you begin, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence, I believe, is misconstruing the Rules. The Rules have a presumption that an accused will be detained absent exceptional circumstances. I have no independent knowledge about whether or not that is different in the former Yugoslavia or in other countries, but our Rules are very clear, that there is a presumption that an accused will not be released absent exceptional circumstances. I think that presumption is justified for this Tribunal because we are dealing with the most serious cases, because if they are not the most serious violations of International Humanitarian Law, we do not have jurisdiction over them to begin with; and (2) because we do not have the normal police resources of a national state, it is much harder for us to monitor accused and get them if they attempt to flee. There is nothing in the Rules in response to your specific question, Judge McDonald, that indicates that the Court can or should consider the merits of the case. I think for the Court to do this, the Rules would have to be amended to permit that and to permit some sort of procedure by which this would happen. In that regard, I want to emphasise to the court that this indictment in addition to being brought by the Prosecution has been confirmed by a judge. So there has already been a finding that there is at least prima facie evidence that, in fact, the accused in this case is responsible for the crimes in the indictment. In this case there are not exceptional circumstances. This defendant is in the same position as all defendants who are now before the Court or who might later on be before the Court. In particular, this Court cannot be satisfied that there is no risk of flight. In this regard, I will point out that we do not even know exactly what country the defendant would go to. He has been living for a number of years, except for a period during the war, in Austria and Germany. I do not even know if they would accept him into their country again. Austria and Germany is where his prior business was. So I do not know how going back to Bosnia would even help him with his financial considerations, but I do not believe those are even necessary for this Court to decide. Thus far there has been no guarantee or any way that this Court could be satisfied that he will not flee. He could easily flee to a country which does not co‑operate with the Tribunal. Even if he does go to a country which does co‑operate with the Tribunal, we cannot be sure that the country would be able to find the accused if he decided to flee and, even if he was found by this country, it is a matter of months and some significant amount of difficulty to actually get the person to the Tribunal. We would strenuously object to his being released on any kind of bail bond. We do not believe in a crime of this magnitude and given the circumstances here, including that, we are not going to have any reliable way of knowing the defendant's exact financial resources, either from his own finances or others. We would not know what to do. But even besides that, I do not believe in this kind of serious case there is any amount of money that would guarantee that he would appear for trial. Similarly, I do not believe that this Court can be satisfied that the accused does not pose a danger to potential witnesses and victims. For that reason, we would ask that this motion be denied immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Stephen has suggested that, perhaps, we can set aside at least for the purposes of this application the whole question of the identification card that has been submitted by the Prosecutor that contains the name other than Delalic but is the photo of Delalic. Ms. Residovic said that was prepared by some individual legally done in order to allow persons to cross Serbian and Croat, I believe, lines. So I just would like your position regarding that. Where did you get this? I have seen it, of course. That and the other attachment is not in my native tongue, so I do not know what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have not seen the document that the Defence referred to about this false identity document. We got it from the German and Austrian authorities who conducted searches at various places, including residents and businesses of this accused and other accused. My information is not the same as the Defence counsel's about the source of this document. Because I do not know the specifics of the circumstances of the witness, I am reluctant to say more, especially without having seen the documents of the accused that she refers to, but I do believe that at the time this document was not done properly and it was because at the time the accused or shortly thereafter was fleeing from Bosnian authorities. Again, I do not know all the ins and outs of what was going on at that time because some of that, most of it, is not relevant to the specific case before us but, in fact, I do not think it is necessary for the Court to consider the forged document or false document because I believe the motion can be denied without it, but my information is not the same as Defence counsel's.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The accused in the papers that it filed has said that Mr. Delalic from 1970 until his arrest has lived and worked in the Federal Republic of Germany and the Republic of Austria, except for the time that he was in the Republic of Bosnia‑Herzegovina for eight months. "He works hard to support his family, had 60 employees of his business and after his arrest 20 workers had to be dismissed. There are no criminal proceedings against him other than the ones by this Tribunal; that the Republic of Austria, the Republic of Germany and the Republic of Bosnia‑Herzegovina have co‑operated with the Tribunal". The matters relating to his son and daughter living in Belgrade have been addressed; that witnesses and victims of the crimes are located in other countries and are not accessible to Mr. Delalic; that he is not in a position to interfere with any evidence. I gather, Ms McHenry, it is your position that these do not establish exceptional circumstances and, further, that the Defence has failed to demonstrate that the accused will appear for trial, that is, he is not likely to flee, and that because of the nature of the offences charged and based on his papers that he has failed to demonstrate that he would pose a danger to any victim, witness or other person. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is my position, your Honour. With respect to some of the specific points argued by the accused, we would take issue with several of them. For instance, although it is the case that Austria has pledged co‑operation with the Tribunal, at least as of my last information a couple of months ago, they had not passed any implementing legislation yet. Similarly, with respect to the idea that the witness and victims are located in countries and places which are totally inaccessible to Mr. Delalic, some of the witnesses are in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So, if that is the place that he would go back to, I would disagree with that. So there are some of the specifics. For instance, the fact that his business was in Germany and Austria, given that I do not believe that he could go back there, I think that is irrelevant in any event. So, in general, I would say even if all these things were true they would not demonstrate exceptional circumstances. In fact, however, there are some of them that we do not agree with.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, where is Mr. Delalic's business? Have you made that clear in the papers that you have submitted? Do you consider that that is an important matter for the Trial Chamber to know and ruling on the motion for provisional release?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Without consulting Mr. Delalic, I cannot give you an immediate answer to that. I think that the company that is in financial difficulties right now is in Austria, and also he was working in a company in Germany. But, if you will allow me, I would like to consult with Mr. Delalic and he could directly answer this question. I have also not spoken about the witnesses. Out of 22 detainees of Celebici, only two that Mr. Delalic for which he intervened to be released say something about his responsibility. Another five heard that he was a significant person in authority and the others had not even heard of him. The detainees from Celebici have published a book about their experience. In '93 there was that Helsinki Watch document where it states that Bosnia‑Herzegovina was not hiding existence of its detention centres, and the name of Zejnil Delalic does not appear in this document. So, your Honours, I want to say that his influence on the witnesses, those that do not even know him, have not heard of him, to whom he has done nothing and they have not even heard of him, or you should rely on two witnesses who have pointed to him and they themselves are criminals as members of HVO. As far as the forged document, ID document, is concerned, I can give you assurances of the MUP of Bosnia‑Herzegovina from which we asked this document based on today's proceedings. Unfortunately, they are both in the Bosnian language, but if the Tribunal finds it pertinent, it can be translated. But this document from MUP states how this document was issued, under what number and in co‑operation with the army and HVO, so that people could move freely through those territories. As you know, there have been two attempts on his life, precisely from persons who are claiming, who are alleging, that he was a person in authority.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may submit that document, if you wish, although I agree with Judge Stephen, I think that we could, perhaps, disregard for the purposes of this application this question of the identification document that was raised by the Prosecutor. I personally would be interested in knowing more about Mr. Delalic's contacts with a community, with a country. In your paper, in your application, you indicate or you just state from 1970 until his arrest he has lived in and worked in the Federal Republic of Germany and the Federal Republic of Austria. Ties with a community, in my experience, has been one of the factors, at least as it relates to the likelihood of flight. I do not have a clear picture of that. Where is his business? Is it still in operation? Would he go back to that business and operate that business? That is something that, perhaps, we can discuss this evening. Where is he proposing to live after this, Judge Stephen has suggested? We will not continue the hearing on the provisional release this evening, but in the interests of time you will be able to communicate with Mr. Delalic and then inform the Trial Chamber of that limited matter this evening. Is that acceptable, Ms McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then I would suggest that the Prosecution and ‑‑ one other matter. We have this statement then from the Netherlands and each party has received it. We will consider that to the extent that it is helpful along with our application which we will take under advisement. I would suggest in the time that you have before we meet this evening that, Ms McHenry and Ms. Residovic, you get together and be able to list succinctly what is outstanding, Ms Residovic, what you consider the Prosecution has not complied with, be able to give us a list of those matters so that we can deal with them and understand them quickly and succinctly and, perhaps, we will not even have a need for that meeting this afternoon because everything will be resolved. That would be nice also. But we will then adjourn and we will have a status conference then at, say, 5.45 and that will be in camera and Mr. Delalic will be present as well.
